clue.text: Film Aussie's welcome to screen about animal

indicators.note: to screen something is to shield or enclose it, so the greeting wraps around the other pieces

parts.note: G'day is the Australian greeting
round can mean about, as in 'round the house'
a hog is a pig

explanation.surface: A film shows an Australian saying hello before a picture about an animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'screen' suggests a cinema showing; here it means enclose, so the Australian greeting is split to wrap around the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Groundhog Day is the 1993 Bill Murray comedy about a man reliving one day.

clue.text: A pope's man metamorphosed in a novel

parts.note: Gregor Samsa is the man transformed into an insect in Kafka's The Metamorphosis

indicators.note: novel means new, so the two little words are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone belonging to a pope undergoes a transformation in a work of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a noun completing the Kafka reference; it is an adjective signalling the anagram of IN A, giving IAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Gregorian describes something belonging to a Pope Gregory, such as the calendar or chant; the possessive makes it adjectival.

clue.text: Away fixture is better

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the verb, with its object understood

parts.note: out means away, as in 'out of the office'
a fixture is a scheduled sporting match

explanation.surface: A sports report says the team's away game is the stronger.
explanation.definitionFit: To outmatch someone is to surpass or outdo them.

clue.text: Jog in a revealing state around Germany's capital

indicators.note: around tells us the bare word goes on either side of the letter

parts.note: someone nude is wholly revealed, wearing nothing

indicators.note: a capital letter is a word's first, so this takes the start of the country's name

explanation.surface: A jogger runs about Berlin without clothes on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' tempts BERLIN; it means the first letter of Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: To jog someone's elbow or memory is to give it a small push or prod.

clue.text: Point grasped by star American historian

indicators.note: something grasped is held in the hands, so the point sits within the other two pieces

parts.note: the star of a story is its hero
US stands for the United States, so American
a dot is a small point

explanation.surface: A US celebrity has a firm grip on the argument being made.
explanation.definitionFit: Herodotus, the Greek writer of the fifth century BC, is called the father of history.

clue.text: Almost caught flu

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: gripped means held or caught

explanation.surface: A patient nearly came down with influenza.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught' reads as catching a cold; it is GRIPPED, losing its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Grippe is an old word, from French, for influenza.

clue.text: Debates lacking energy in the Guardian

indicators.note: lacking means going without, so one letter drops out of the word

parts.note: to argue is to debate
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Discussions in the newspaper have gone flat and listless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Guardian' reads as the newspaper printing this puzzle; it is the mythical watchman.
explanation.definitionFit: Argus was the hundred-eyed giant set as a watchman in Greek myth, so his name means a vigilant guard.

clue.text: Return of Puck with wonderful puzzle

indicators.note: a return is a coming back, so the joined pieces are read backwards

parts.note: Puck is the mischievous sprite or elf of A Midsummer Night's Dream
fab is short for fabulous, wonderful

explanation.surface: The comeback of a hockey puck makes for a marvellous brainteaser.
explanation.definitionFit: To baffle someone is to perplex or bewilder them.

clue.text: Mechanical saw bishop lifted

indicators.note: lifted means raised up, and in a down entry the pieces then read upwards

parts.note: a saw is an old saying, a motto
B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: A mechanic noticed a clergyman being raised up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'saw' looks like a verb or tool; it is a proverb. 'Mechanical' is a noun here: Shakespeare's 'rude mechanicals' are the workmen in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: Nick Bottom the weaver is one of the amateur actors, called mechanicals, in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

clue.text: Practised fitting coats of Parisian

indicators.note: to coat something is to cover it all over, so the outer word surrounds the French one

parts.note: apt means suitable or fitting
de is French for of

explanation.surface: A Paris tailor is experienced at fitting overcoats.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone adept is skilled through long experience, highly proficient.

clue.text: Bravado deserted guilty party

parts.note: erring means doing wrong, so guilty
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A show of bravado abandoned the culprit.
explanation.definitionFit: Derring-do is reckless heroic daring, the stuff of swashbuckling tales.

clue.text: It's viewed as what followed Labour's Callaghan era?

parts.note: Michael Foot succeeded James Callaghan as leader of Britain's Labour Party in 1980
an age is an era

explanation.surface: A political history asks what the period after Callaghan looked like.
explanation.walkthrough: James Callaghan was a 1970s British Labour prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Footage is filmed material, something watched on screen.

clue.text: Store silicon in warehouse

indicators.note: in places the element symbol within the word for a storage building

parts.note: a depot is a warehouse
Si is the chemical symbol for silicon

explanation.surface: Chips are being kept in a storage building.
explanation.definitionFit: To deposit something is to put it away for safekeeping.

clue.text: Rough copies spread in clergyman's office

indicators.note: rough means roughly done, unpolished, so these letters are worked into another arrangement

parts.note: pâté is a spread for toast

explanation.surface: Draft documents are scattered about a vicar's study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spread' looks like the anagram signal; it is PATE, and 'Rough' rearranges COPIES into EPISCO.
explanation.definitionFit: The episcopate is the post, or term of office, of a bishop.

clue.text: It may be shot or longer drink, holding a party

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the drink goes round the letter

parts.note: a pint is a longer drink than a half
a ball is a formal party

explanation.surface: Someone is offered a shot of spirits or a long drink at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot' suggests a measure of spirits, set against the longer drink; it means fired.
explanation.definitionFit: A paintball is a pellet of dye fired from a gas gun in the combat game.

clue.text: Ancient Middle East kingdom, way back

indicators.note: back means going backwards, so the word for way is read in reverse

parts.note: a mode is a way of doing something

explanation.surface: An old kingdom of the region is followed a long way into history.
explanation.definitionFit: Edom was a biblical kingdom south of the Dead Sea.

clue.text: Drug from figure with a short amount of coke

parts.note: a digit is a numeral, a figure

indicators.note: short means cut short, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: a line is a dose of cocaine laid out to be snorted

explanation.surface: A dealer gets a drug from someone with a little cocaine.
explanation.definitionFit: Digitalin is a heart drug extracted from foxglove leaves.

clue.text: Composer from Britain penning number one

indicators.note: penning means shutting in, as sheep are in a pen, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: Albion is an old poetic name for Britain
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A British composer writes a hit single.
explanation.walkthrough: 'number one' reads as a hit record; it is N inside ALBION, then I.
explanation.definitionFit: Tomaso Albinoni was a Venetian Baroque composer, credited with the famous Adagio in G minor.

clue.text: Frank or Stuart more than once plugs American news channel

indicators.note: the name is plugged inside the words twice, once across 'American news' and once in 'channel'

explanation.surface: A presenter repeatedly promotes a US news network.
explanation.walkthrough: The name sits inside 'American news' and again inside 'channel'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Frank was the Dutch wartime diarist, and Queen Anne was the last Stuart monarch: two people sharing that first name.

clue.text: People staying dry without a bit of clothing in scripture

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so the two letters surround the garment

parts.note: AA is Alcoholics Anonymous, whose members stay off alcohol
a vest is an item of clothing

explanation.surface: Teetotallers go short of clothes in a sacred text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' seems to mean lacking; it means outside.
explanation.definitionFit: The Avesta is the sacred book of Zoroastrianism.

clue.text: Early period in 1 across?

definitions.meaning: dawn, the earliest part of the day
1 across is the first entry, or light, in the grid

explanation.surface: Dawn breaks in the film about the same day repeating.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossword answers are called lights, so the 1 across entry is the opening one, as dawn opens the day.

clue.text: Refuse to carry hard kind of metal

indicators.note: to carry means to hold within, so the letter for hard goes inside

parts.note: trash is refuse, rubbish
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Someone declines to carry a heavy load of metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' reads as a verb; it is the noun meaning rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrash is a fast, aggressive style of heavy metal music.

clue.text: Hammer in part of building work

parts.note: a wall is part of a building
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A hammer is used in part of a building job.
explanation.definitionFit: To wallop is to strike hard or thrash, as one may hammer an opponent.

clue.text: Inclination to leave out the front entrance

definitions.note: the verb en-TRANCE, to put in a trance, not the noun meaning a way in

indicators.note: leaving out the front means the word loses its first letter

parts.note: a penchant is a liking or inclination

explanation.surface: People tend to exit by the main door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entrance' reads as a doorway; it is the verb meaning delight.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance someone is to captivate or delight them.

clue.text: Naughty so-and-so, say, twirling bum

definitions.note: used as a verb, to scrounge

parts.note: a cad is a man who behaves dishonourably

indicators.note: twirling means spinning round, so the two letters are turned backwards

parts.note: eg, for example, means say

explanation.surface: A mischievous rascal is wiggling his backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bum' looks like a noun for the backside; it is the verb meaning scrounge.
explanation.definitionFit: To cadge is to beg or scrounge something for free.

clue.text: Theatre about to host prancing Tina Turner?

indicators.note: hosting means receiving guests inside, so the shuffled name goes within
about means turned round, so the theatre word is read backwards

parts.note: rep is short for repertory theatre

indicators.note: prancing means capering about, so the letters of the name move around

explanation.surface: A theatre is about to stage a show with Tina Turner dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' flips REP into PER, and 'prancing' turns TINA into AINT. 'Tina Turner' reads as the singer; only 'Turner' defines, as J.M.W. Turner.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. W. Turner was the great English painter of landscapes and seascapes; the question mark marks a definition by example.

clue.text: Letters of Euripides showing devout image

parts.note: pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet, the language Euripides wrote in
eta is another Greek letter, so a second letter of the playwright's alphabet

explanation.surface: A Greek playwright's correspondence reveals a pious picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' tempts a pick from the name; it means two letters of the Greek alphabet, PI and ETA.
explanation.definitionFit: A pietà is a religious painting or sculpture of the Virgin Mary holding the dead Christ.

clue.text: Curiously wild at greeting a crashing bore

indicators.note: curiously means in an odd way, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: ave is Latin for hail, a greeting

explanation.surface: Oddly, someone gets wild at being greeted by a terribly dull person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crashing bore' reads as a tedious person; a bore is a tidal surge up a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A bore is a tidal surge up an estuary, and a breaking one crashes like a huge sea wave.

clue.text: Eyeballs possibly globes, but not black

definitions.note: the verb, as in stares at

indicators.note: possibly means the letters might be arranged another way
but not means one letter is excluded from the pool before rearranging

parts.note: B is the pencil abbreviation for black

explanation.surface: Eyeballs are perhaps round globes, but they are not dark.
explanation.walkthrough: GLOBES without B leaves GLOES, which is rearranged. 'Eyeballs' looks like a plural noun; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To eyeball someone is to stare at them, just as to ogle is to look lecherously.

clue.text: At lido, pose in pants? It's what strippers do

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the preceding letters are in a mess

explanation.surface: A sunbather poses in underwear at the open-air pool, like a stripper.
explanation.walkthrough: A lido is a British public open-air pool. 'pants' looks like underwear; it means rubbish, a jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Despoliation is plundering, stripping a place of its valuables, so it is the work of looters.
